extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of American politics; educated general readers interested in government and party systems
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and guidance for writing or analysing the American party system and related political institutions — what to cover, what sources to use, and how to present the material (history, doctrines, organization, machinery, public opinion, corruption, campaigns, regional differences, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Political Parties and their History
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin with the origins and development of parties (the author locates the history of American party life at the Constitutional Convention of 1787 and follows centrifugal vs. centripetal tendencies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain early tendencies (centrifugal v. centripetal), trace how personalities and events (e.g., Hamilton, Jefferson, ratification debates) produced party divisions; show how parties arose from circumstances of the nation rather than being mere transplants of English Whigs/Tories. Use historical episodes (e.g., Louisiana purchase, Missouri Compromise) to illustrate tendencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe the Parties of To-day (contemporary doctrines)
rubrics_metrics.description: Set out the doctrines, professed principles, and practical positions of the present parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relate present doctrines back to historical roots and leaders; distinguish professed principles from practical tendencies (e.g., tendency toward organization when principles weaken). Include how parties position themselves on key policy areas (trade, federal power, slavery in historical example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of the Parties (social bases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyse the social, regional, economic, and religious composition of parties (who follows each party and why).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify social groups (farmers, merchants, clergy), regional strengths (South, New England, middle States, West), and interest-based alignments (commercial interests, manufacturing, agricultural) and explain tactical/organizational causes for alignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Party Organization as Complement to Constitutional Institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat party organization and association as a necessary complement to constitutional/legal institutions — parties transmit motive power and direct governmental action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When accounting for government functioning, include party machinery and organization as part of the system; explain how party ingenuity turns constitutional provisions to unforeseen uses and shapes practical politics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Sources — variety and empirical grounding
rubrics_metrics.description: Base description of party workings on a wide variety of 'flying and floating' sources (newspaper paragraphs, conversation with acquaintances, impressions from incidents and anecdotes) in addition to books and documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admit limits of documentary sources for daily party mechanics; supplement with first‑hand observation, contemporary press, interviews, and anecdotes while being cautious about the reliability and possible gaps of such materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartiality and Perspective — stranger's advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim for an impartial, judicial description of the actual daily working of parties; a 'stranger' perspective can compensate for a native's familiarity and blind spots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that native writers may miss what strangers find perplexing; attempt to avoid partisanship; present daily practical workings rather than merely constitutional theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Machine and its Functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyse the party 'machine' — its organization, functions, duties, and role in converting numbers into power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe what the machine 'has to do' and 'how the machine works' (its operations, mechanisms, and tasks). Discuss development of mechanisms as substitute for spontaneity and how organization can make numbers omnipotent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rings and Bosses (bossism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine the existence, structure, and effects of rings and bosses at national and local levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace how rings and bosses operate, their extension into localities, examples of bossdom, and the methods by which they exert influence over nominations, appointments and public resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spoils and Patronage
rubrics_metrics.description: Study the patronage/spoils system as a central element of party organisation — public office as reward for adherents of the President/party in power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain the principle that public office is to be enjoyed only by party adherents, show how spoils motivate organisation, and connect patronage to party cohesion and corruption risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elections and Their Machinery
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the practical machinery of elections — voting methods, organisation on election day, ballot practices and their administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detail technical and logistical aspects of voting, how electoral machinery interacts with party organisation, and how devices can be used to influence outcomes (and be sources of corruption or reform).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corruption and the War against Bossdom
rubrics_metrics.description: Address corruption tied to party structures and machines and the movements and reforms aimed at countering bossdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document forms of corruption (e.g., financial scandals, vote manipulation), analyze causes rooted in patronage and machine incentives, and present historical reform efforts and legislation (primaries, anti‑boss campaigns).

rubrics_metrics.name: National Nominating Conventions and Their Workings
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyse the institutions and practical workings of national nominating conventions and their role in candidate selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain convention procedures, the realpolitik behind nominations, internal struggles, how conventions function in practice (not only formal rules), and their interaction with party machines and campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Presidential Campaign and Presidential Issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Study the dynamics of presidential campaigns and the substantive issues that dominate presidential elections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider campaign organisation, messaging, mobilization of voters, the role of issues versus personalities, and how national issues shape electoral strategy and party coalitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public Opinion — Nature and Government by Opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat public opinion as a distinct subject: its nature, how it is formed, and how government is influenced or governed by public sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss organs of opinion (press, orators), national characteristics shaping opinion, classes' influence, local/regional variations (East, West, South), and the mechanisms by which public opinion acts on political institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organs and Channels of Public Opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and evaluate the principal organs (newspapers, pamphlets, orators, associations) through which opinion is formed and transmitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the reach, biases, and effectiveness of different organs; relate them to party operations and to how parties mobilize or shape opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional and Class Variations in Opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyse how regional types (East, West, South) and social classes influence public opinion and partisan alignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map differences in temperament, issues, and political culture across regions and classes and show how these differences are exploited or mediated by parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strengths and Failures of Public Opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Balance analysis of where public opinion succeeds in guiding politics and where it fails (tyranny of the majority, fatalism of the multitude, areas where it is effective).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate both constructive and dangerous effects: e.g., majority tyranny, susceptibility to sensationalism, but also capacity to check elites; give examples and historical cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Illustrations and Case Studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ concrete case-studies and illustrations (e.g., Tammany Ring, Philadelphia Gas Ring, Kearneyism) to illuminate abstract points about parties and corruption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include vivid local or historical examples to show mechanisms at work, to ground theoretical claims, and to provide empirical demonstration of organisational features and abuses.
